analysis.one_liner: Rolls back consumer-disclosure rules, legal remedies, and regulatory approvals for banks, savings institutions, and credit unions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 1996 with zero cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a large deregulation bill for the banking industry. It would have cut back consumer protections in mortgage and credit law — weakening anti-kickback rules, trimming Truth in Lending and Truth in Savings disclosures and liability, removing second mortgages from settlement-process protections, and letting bank affiliates freely share customer information with only an opt-out. It also would have exempted many banks from merger and branch approval requirements, let banks that self-test for lending discrimination keep the results out of court, loosen insider-lending rules for bank executives, and restructure the deposit insurance funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Depository institutions — banks, savings associations, and credit unions — gain the most: less paperwork, no prior regulatory approval for many mergers, branches, and ATMs, reduced disclosure and liability under consumer credit laws, freer sharing of customer data among affiliates, expanded authority to sell insurance and annuities, and easier insider lending. Executives and directors of those institutions specifically gain from relaxed insider-lending and interlock rules.

how_it_helps.text: Well-capitalized, well-managed holding companies could start new activities and acquire banks or savings associations without prior Federal Reserve approval, and banks could open branches and ATMs without applications — cutting the time and cost of expansion and consolidation.

The bill reduces bank compliance costs under consumer laws: it repeals civil liability for violating Truth in Savings disclosure rules, lets the Federal Reserve exempt whole classes of transactions from Truth in Lending, removes second mortgages from the settlement-process law (RESPA), and raises the asset threshold for exemption from Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reporting from $10 million to $50 million.

It shields lenders whose voluntary self-tests find discriminatory lending: those results could not be obtained or used against the lender in a legal proceeding if it took corrective action, and agencies would not have to refer such cases to the Attorney General.

Bank executives and directors gain directly: the bill lets member banks extend $100,000 home equity lines to executives, relaxes insider-lending limits tied to employee benefit plans, repeals the written debt report requirement, raises the ceiling on credit union loans to officials without board approval from $10,000 to $50,000, and loosens rules on directors serving competing institutions.

It recapitalizes the savings association deposit insurance fund (SAIF) through a special assessment and merges it with the bank insurance fund, addressing an industry-wide funding problem while limiting future assessments to what is needed to maintain the reserve ratio.

analysis.who_pays: Bank and mortgage customers would bear the cost: fewer and simpler disclosures (including dropping the requirement that adjustable-rate mortgage disclosures show how a rate change affects payments), no civil liability for deposit-disclosure violations, a one-year limit on claims over mortgage servicing and escrow handling, criminal penalties for settlement kickbacks applied only to willful violations, and customer data flowing freely among bank affiliates with only a pre-emptive opt-out. Regulators and fair-lending enforcers would also lose information and approval authority.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals civil liability for deposit institutions that fail to meet Truth in Savings disclosure requirements, leaving consumers with no private remedy when they are misled about account terms.

It removes second mortgages from RESPA protections, weakens the criminal standard for settlement-service kickbacks to willful violations only, and shortens the time limit for suing over mortgage servicing and escrow violations to one year — making it harder for borrowers to challenge abusive practices.

Allowing unlimited information sharing among bank affiliates (with only an opt-out before data is first shared) would expose customers' financial records across an entire banking family, a privacy rollback that predated the later Gramm-Leach-Bliley notice framework.

Privileging lender self-tests that uncover discrimination, and barring applicants and agencies from using those results in court, would remove some of the strongest evidence of illegal lending bias while formally encouraging voluntary compliance.

Raising the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act exemption from $10 million to $50 million in assets would take thousands of smaller lenders out of the public reporting system that lets communities detect redlining.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some pieces are defensible on their own terms — a single unified mortgage disclosure format, updated leasing-disclosure rules, and recapitalizing the savings-insurance fund protect depositors and could genuinely simplify paperwork. But the bill bundles those items with substantial rollbacks of consumer legal rights: liability repeal, shorter limitations periods, weaker kickback penalties, privileged self-test evidence, and freer affiliate data sharing. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the simplification benefits are inseparable from the liability and enforcement carve-outs, and that the bill's own small-business lending study (Title IV) was an untested promise that deregulation would trickle down to borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-September 1996, sent to the House Banking Committee the same day, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: House Banking Committee Chairman James Leach introduced the bill by request on September 16, 1996, late in the second session of the 104th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services the same day; no further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, or vote — is recorded.
Not a single member cosponsored the bill.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bank and mortgage customers are better off because the bill died: the consumer disclosure rules, legal remedies, and fair-lending evidence rights it would have trimmed all remained on the books. The banking industry gained nothing from this bill, though much of its agenda resurfaced in later deregulation legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank customers, who kept existing protections

for.name: Rep. James A. Leach
for.role: Chairman, House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill by request on September 16, 1996; it was referred to his own committee, which took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor vote was ever taken and no one cosponsored the bill, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose was to cut these institutions' regulatory burden: no prior approval for many mergers, branches, and ATMs, fewer examinations, relaxed audit and reporting rules, and trimmed consumer-law liability. The gains come largely at customers' expense, though the SAIF recapitalization also served the industry's shared interest in a solvent deposit insurance fund.

They would get a carve-out letting employers pay employees for referrals, a willfulness requirement for criminal kickback penalties, removal of second mortgages from RESPA, and a one-year limit on servicing and escrow claims — all reducing their exposure to borrower suits and enforcement.

Title VII broadens bank holding companies' authority to sell insurance and tax-deferred annuities and treats annuity sales as an insurance agency activity, letting banks deepen their entry into insurance distribution at the expense of independent agents.

The bill raises the ceiling on loans to credit union officials without board approval from $10,000 to $50,000, but also prohibits credit unions from accepting financial support from government-sponsored enterprises serving their membership.
